The third group of foreigners to arrive in Hawaii were from China. Chinese workers on Western trading ships settled in Hawaii starting in 1789. In 1820, the first American missionaries arrived to preach Christianity and teach the Hawaiians Western ways.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Charles_Williams-189) As of 2015, a large proportion of Hawaii's population have Asian ancestry—especially Filipino, Japanese and Chinese. Many are descendants of immigrants brought to work on the sugarcane plantations in the mid-to-late 19th century. The first 153 Japanese immigrants arrived in Hawaii on June 19, 1868. They were not approved by the then-current Japanese government because the contract was between a broker and the [Tokugawa shogunate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokugawa_shogunate "Tokugawa shogunate")—by then replaced by the [Meiji Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meiji_Restoration "Meiji Restoration"). The first Japanese current-government-approved immigrants arrived on February 9, 1885, after Kalākaua's petition to [Emperor Meiji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Meiji "Emperor Meiji") when Kalākaua visited Japan in 1881.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Goto-190)[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Wao+Lani-191)

Almost 13,000 Portuguese migrants had arrived by 1899; they also worked on the sugarcane plantations.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Hoffman-192) By 1901, more than 5,000 Puerto Ricans were living in Hawaii.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-L%C3%B3pez-193)

### Languages

[![Image 27](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/Portuguese_immigrant_family_in_Hawaii_during_the_19th_century.jpg/250px-Portuguese_immigrant_family_in_Hawaii_during_the_19th_century.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Portuguese_immigrant_family_in_Hawaii_during_the_19th_century.jpg)

Many [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_people "Portuguese people") immigrants were [Azorean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azores "Azores") or [Madeiran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madeira "Madeira"). They brought with them [Catholicism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") and Portuguese language and cuisine.

English and [Hawaiian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_language "Hawaiian language") are listed as Hawaii's official languages in the state's 1978 constitution, in Article XV, Section 4.[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-194) However, the use of Hawaiian is limited because the constitution specifies that "Hawaiian shall be required for public acts and transactions only as provided by law". [Hawaiʻi Creole English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_Pidgin "Hawaiian Pidgin"), locally referred to as "Pidgin", is the native language of many native residents and is a second language for many others.[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-195)

The 2000 Census found that 73.4% of Hawaii residents age 5 and older exclusively spoke English at home.[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-mla-196) According to the 2008 American Community Survey, 74.6% of Hawaii's residents older than 5 spoke only English at home.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-factfinder.census.gov-187) In their homes, 21.0% of state residents speak an additional [Asian language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languages_of_Asia "Languages of Asia"), 2.6% speak Spanish, 1.6% speak other [Indo-European languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-European_language "Indo-European language") and 0.2% speak another language.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-factfinder.census.gov-187)

After English, other languages popularly spoken in the state are [Tagalog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagalog_language "Tagalog language"), [Ilocano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilocano_language "Ilocano language"), and Japanese.[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-197) 5.4% of residents speak Tagalog, which includes non-native speakers of [Filipino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filipino_language "Filipino language"), a Tagalog-based national and co-official language of the Philippines; 5.0% speak Japanese and 4.0% speak Ilocano; 1.2% speak Chinese, 1.7% speak Hawaiian; 1.7% speak Spanish; 1.6% speak [Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_language "Korean language"); and 1.0% speak [Samoan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samoan_language "Samoan language").[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-mla-196)

#### Hawaiian

The Hawaiian language has about 2,000 native speakers, about 0.15% of the total population.[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Lyovin-198) According to the [United States Census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census "United States Census"), there were more than 24,000 total speakers of the language in Hawaii in 2006–2008.[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Census_Bureau_Hawaiian_Speaker_estimate-199) Hawaiian is a Polynesian member of the [Austronesian language family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austronesian_languages "Austronesian languages").[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Lyovin-198) It is closely related to other [Polynesian languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_languages "Polynesian languages"), such as [Marquesan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marquesan_language "Marquesan language"), [Tahitian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tahitian_language "Tahitian language"), [Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_language "Māori language"), [Rapa Nui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapa_Nui_language "Rapa Nui language") (the language of [Easter Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easter_Island "Easter Island")), and less closely to [Samoan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samoan_language "Samoan language") and [Tongan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tongan_language "Tongan language").[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-200)

According to Schütz, the Marquesans colonized the archipelago in roughly 300 CE[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-201) and were later followed by waves of seafarers from the [Society Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_Islands "Society Islands"), [Samoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samoa "Samoa") and [Tonga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonga "Tonga").[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-202) These Polynesians remained in the islands; they eventually became the Hawaiian people and [their languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_language#Family_and_origin "Hawaiian language") evolved into the Hawaiian language.[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-203) Kimura and Wilson say: "[l]inguists agree that Hawaiian is closely related to Eastern Polynesian, with a particularly strong link in the Southern Marquesas, and a secondary link in Tahiti, which may be explained by voyaging between the Hawaiian and Society Islands".[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-204)

Before the arrival of Captain James Cook, the Hawaiian language had no written form. That form was developed mainly by American Protestant missionaries between 1820 and 1826 who assigned to the Hawaiian phonemes letters from the Latin alphabet. Interest in Hawaiian increased significantly in the late 20th century. With the help of the Office of Hawaiian Affairs, specially designated immersion schools in which all subjects would be taught in Hawaiian were established. The [University of Hawaiʻi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Hawai%CA%BBi "University of Hawaiʻi") developed a Hawaiian-language graduate studies program. Municipal codes were altered to favor Hawaiian place and street names for new civic developments.[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-205)

Hawaiian distinguishes between [long and short vowel sounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vowel_length "Vowel length"). In modern practice, vowel length is indicated with a [macron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macron_(diacritic) "Macron (diacritic)") (_[kahakō](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian\_language#Orthography "Hawaiian language")_). Hawaiian-language newspapers (_nūpepa_) published from 1834 to 1948 and traditional native speakers of Hawaiian generally omit the marks in their own writing. The ʻokina and kahakō are intended to capture the proper pronunciation of Hawaiian words.[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-206) The Hawaiian language uses the [glottal stop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glottal_stop "Glottal stop") (_[ʻOkina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%CA%BBOkina "ʻOkina")_) as a consonant. It is written as a symbol similar to the apostrophe or left-hanging (opening) single quotation mark.[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-207)

The keyboard layout used for Hawaiian is [QWERTY](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QWERTY "QWERTY").[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-208)

#### Hawaiian Pidgin

[![Image 28](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Hermann_A._Widemann_and_family%2C_ca._1850s.jpg/250px-Hermann_A._Widemann_and_family%2C_ca._1850s.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hermann_A._Widemann_and_family,_ca._1850s.jpg)

Mixed Hawaiian/European-American family in Honolulu, 1850s

**Hawaiian Pidgin**, officially known as [Hawaiʻi Creole English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_Pidgin "Hawaiian Pidgin") (HCE), is a creole language that emerged in [Hawaiʻi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_(island) "Hawaii (island)") during the 19th century as a means of communication among diverse groups working on sugarcane plantations.[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-:7-209) Its lexicon is primarily derived from [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language"), with significant contributions from [Hawaiian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_language "Hawaiian language"), [Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"), [Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language"), [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language"), [Ilocano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilocano_language "Ilocano language"), and [Tagalog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagalog_language "Tagalog language").

The development of Hawaiian Pidgin began with [Pidgin Hawaiian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pidgin_Hawaiian "Pidgin Hawaiian"), an earlier pidgin that formed in the 1790s during initial contact between [Native Hawaiians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Hawaiians "Native Hawaiians") and foreigners. As plantation laborers from various countries arrived, a new pidgin based on English evolved to facilitate communication among workers and supervisors.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-210)

By the early 20th century, children of these plantation workers began acquiring **Hawaiian Pidgin** as their first language, leading to its creolization. This transition marked the emergence of HCE as a fully developed creole language.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-211)[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-:7-209)

HCE incorporates Hawaiian words, especially in place names and terms for local flora and fauna. For instance, the Hawaiian term for tuna, "ahi," is commonly used in HCE. Additionally, certain English words have adapted meanings; "aunty" and "uncle" are used to address any respected elder, regardless of familial relation.[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-:8-212)[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-213)[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-214)

Some expressions from HCE have permeated other communities, particularly through surfing culture. Terms like "brah" (brother) and "da kine" (a versatile placeholder term) have gained recognition beyond Hawaiʻi.[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-:8-212)

In 2015, the [U.S. Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau") recognized Hawaiian Pidgin as an official language in Hawaiʻi, reflecting its widespread use among residents. Despite this recognition, debates continue about its role in education and its impact on learning [Standard English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_English "Standard English").[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-215)

#### Hawaiʻi Sign Language

[Hawaiʻi Sign Language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawai%CA%BBi_Sign_Language "Hawaiʻi Sign Language"), a [sign language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sign_language "Sign language") for the Deaf based on the Hawaiian language, has been in use in the islands since the early 1800s. It is dwindling in numbers due to [American Sign Language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Sign_Language "American Sign Language") supplanting HSL through schooling and various other domains.[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-216)

Hawaii is among the most religiously diverse states in the U.S., with one in ten residents practicing a non-Christian faith.[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-219) Roughly one-quarter to half the population identify as unaffiliated and nonreligious, making Hawaii one of the most secular states as well.

Christianity remains the majority religion, represented mainly by various [Protestant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestants "Protestants") groups and [Catholicism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church"). The second-largest religion is [Buddhism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism "Buddhism"), which comprises a larger proportion of the population than in any other state; it is concentrated in the Japanese community. Native Hawaiians continue to engage in traditional religious and spiritual practices today, often adhering to Christian and traditional beliefs at the same time.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-LaDuke_1999-70)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-FLEXNER_2016_307%E2%80%93331-103)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-People_of_the_seventh_fire-99)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-nps.gov-104)

The [Cathedral Church of Saint Andrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathedral_Church_of_Saint_Andrew_(Honolulu) "Cathedral Church of Saint Andrew (Honolulu)") in Honolulu was formally the seat of the [Hawaiian Reformed Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Hawaii "Church of Hawaii"), a province of the [Anglican Communion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Communion "Anglican Communion") that had been the state church of the Kingdom of Hawaii; it subsequently merged into the [Episcopal Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Church_(USA) "Episcopal Church (USA)") in the 1890s following the overthrow of the Kingdom of Hawaii, becoming the seat of the [Episcopal Diocese of Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Diocese_of_Hawaii "Episcopal Diocese of Hawaii"). The [Cathedral Basilica of Our Lady of Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathedral_Basilica_of_Our_Lady_of_Peace "Cathedral Basilica of Our Lady of Peace") and the [Co-Cathedral of Saint Theresa of the Child Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Co-Cathedral_of_Saint_Theresa_of_the_Child_Jesus_(Honolulu,_Hawaii) "Co-Cathedral of Saint Theresa of the Child Jesus (Honolulu, Hawaii)") serve as seats of the [Diocese of Honolulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Diocese_of_Honolulu "Roman Catholic Diocese of Honolulu"). The Eastern Orthodox community is centered around the [Saints Constantine and Helen Greek Orthodox Cathedral of the Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saints_Constantine_and_Helen_Greek_Orthodox_Cathedral_of_the_Pacific_(Honolulu) "Saints Constantine and Helen Greek Orthodox Cathedral of the Pacific (Honolulu)").

The largest religious denominations by membership were the Catholic Church with 249,619 adherents in 2010;[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-www.thearda.com-220) the [Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Church_of_Jesus_Christ_of_Latter-day_Saints_in_Hawaii "The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in Hawaii") with 68,128 adherents in 2009;[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-221) the [United Church of Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Church_of_Christ "United Church of Christ") with 115 congregations and 20,000 members; and the [Southern Baptist Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Baptist_Convention "Southern Baptist Convention") with 108 congregations and 18,000 members.[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-222)[Nondenominational churches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nondenominational_church "Nondenominational church") collectively have 128 congregations and 32,000 members.

### LGBTQ people

Hawaii has had a long history of [LGBTQIA+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBTQIA%2B "LGBTQIA+") identities. _[Māhū](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81h%C5%AB "Māhū")_ ("in the middle") were a precolonial [third gender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_gender "Third gender") with traditional spiritual and social roles, widely respected as healers. Homosexual relationships known as _[aikāne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aik%C4%81ne "Aikāne")_ were widespread and normal in ancient Hawaiian society.[[231]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Murray2002-239)[[232]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Kornblum2011-240)[[233]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Klarman2012-241) Among men, _aikāne_ relationships often began as teens and continued throughout their adult lives, even if they also maintained heterosexual partners.[[234]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-EmberEmber2003-242) While _aikāne_ usually refers to male homosexuality, some stories also refer to women, implying that women may have been involved in _aikāne_ relationships as well.[[235]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Zimmerman2000-243) Journals written by [Captain Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cook "James Cook")'s crew record that many _[aliʻi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali%CA%BBi "Aliʻi")_ (hereditary nobles) also engaged in _aikāne_ relationships, and [Kamehameha the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamehameha_I "Kamehameha I"), the founder and first ruler of the [Kingdom of Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hawaii "Kingdom of Hawaii"), was also known to participate. Cook's second lieutenant and co-astronomer [James King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_King_(Royal_Navy_officer) "James King (Royal Navy officer)") observed that "all the chiefs had them", and recounts that Cook was actually asked by one chief to leave King behind, considering the role a great honor.

Hawaiian scholar [Lilikalā Kameʻeleihiwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lilikal%C4%81_Kame%CA%BBeleihiwa "Lilikalā Kameʻeleihiwa") notes that _aikāne_ served a practical purpose of building mutual trust and cohesion; "If you didn't sleep with a man, how could you trust him when you went into battle? How would you know if he was going to be the warrior that would protect you at all costs, if he wasn't your lover?"[[236]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-mahu-244)

As Western colonial influences intensified in the late 19th and early 20th century, the word _aikāne_ was [expurgated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expurgation "Expurgation") of its original sexual meaning, and in print simply meant "friend". Nonetheless, in Hawaiian language publications its metaphorical meaning can still mean either "friend" or "lover" without stigmatization.[[237]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-245)

A 2012 Gallup poll found that Hawaii had the largest proportion of LGBTQIA+ adults in the U.S., at 5.1%, an estimated 53,966 individuals. The number of same-sex couple households in 2010 was 3,239, representing a 35.5% increase from a decade earlier.[[238]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-246)[[239]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-247) In 2013, Hawaii became the fifteenth U.S. state to legalize same-sex marriage; this reportedly boosted tourism by $217 million.[[240]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-248)

## Economy

[![Image 32: In a pineapple field, a laborer stands with his hat in hand.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/Pineapple_field_near_Honolulu%2C_Hawaii%2C_1907_%28CHS-418%29.jpg/250px-Pineapple_field_near_Honolulu%2C_Hawaii%2C_1907_%28CHS-418%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pineapple_field_near_Honolulu,_Hawaii,_1907_(CHS-418).jpg)

Post-annexation, Hawaii's economy and demographic changes were shaped mostly by growth in the agricultural sector.

[![Image 33: A painting of two white women surfing, circa 1935.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/%27Two_Surfer_Girls%27_by_William_Fulton_Soare%2C_oil_on_canvas%2C_c._1935.JPG/250px-%27Two_Surfer_Girls%27_by_William_Fulton_Soare%2C_oil_on_canvas%2C_c._1935.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%27Two_Surfer_Girls%27_by_William_Fulton_Soare,_oil_on_canvas,_c._1935.JPG)

From the end of World War II onwards, depictions and photographs, such as this one of Hawaii as a tropical, leisure paradise, encouraged the growth of tourism in Hawaii, which eventually became the largest industry of the islands.

[![Image 34: An American soldier at Schofield Barracks.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/US_Navy_111218-N-RI884-097_The_U.S._Pacific_Fleet_Marching_Band_participates_in_a_parade_through_downtown_Waikiki_honoring_Japanese-American_vetera.jpg/250px-US_Navy_111218-N-RI884-097_The_U.S._Pacific_Fleet_Marching_Band_participates_in_a_parade_through_downtown_Waikiki_honoring_Japanese-American_vetera.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:US_Navy_111218-N-RI884-097_The_U.S._Pacific_Fleet_Marching_Band_participates_in_a_parade_through_downtown_Waikiki_honoring_Japanese-American_vetera.jpg)

The U.S. federal government's spending on Hawaii-stationed personnel, installations, and materiel (either directly or through military personnel spending) amounts to Hawaii's second largest source of income after tourism.

The history of Hawaii's economy can be traced through a succession of dominant industries: [sandalwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandalwood "Sandalwood"),[[241]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-249)[whaling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whaling "Whaling"),[[242]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-250) sugarcane, [pineapple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pineapple "Pineapple"), the military, tourism and education. By the 1840s, sugar plantations had gained a strong foothold in the Hawaiian economy, due to a high demand of sugar in the United States and rapid transport via steamships.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-MacLennan_2004_37%E2%80%9362-86) Sugarcane plantations were tightly controlled by American missionary families and businessmen known as "[the Big Five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Five_(Hawaii) "Big Five (Hawaii)")", who monopolized control of the sugar industry's profits.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-MacLennan_2004_37%E2%80%9362-86)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Huard-87) By the time Hawaiian annexation was being considered in 1898, sugarcane producers turned to cultivating tropical fruits like pineapple, which became the principal export for Hawaii's plantation economy.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Huard-87)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-MacLennan_2004_37%E2%80%9362-86)

Since statehood in 1959, tourism has been the largest industry, contributing 24.3% of the gross state product (GSP) in 1997, despite efforts to diversify. In 2025, Hawaii's gross state product was $124.6 billion and the per capita personal income for Hawaii residents was $76,592.[[243]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-251) Hawaiian exports include food and clothing. These industries play a small role in the Hawaiian economy, due to the shipping distance to viable markets, such as the [West Coast of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_of_the_United_States "West Coast of the United States"). The state's food exports include coffee, macadamia nuts, pineapple, livestock, sugarcane, and honey.[[244]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-252)

By weight, honey bees may be the state's most valuable export.[[245]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-253) According to the Hawaii Agricultural Statistics Service, in 2002 agricultural sales were US$370.9 million from diversified agriculture, US$100.6 million from pineapple,[[246]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-254) and US$64.3 million from sugarcane.[[247]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-255) Hawaii's relatively consistent climate has attracted the seed industry, which is able to test three generations of crops per year on the islands, compared with one or two on the mainland.[[248]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-256) Seeds yielded US$264 million in 2012, supporting 1,400 workers.[[249]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-ny1310-257)

As of August 2025, the state's unemployment rate was 2.7%.[[250]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-:9-258) The historically lowest unemployment rate of 2.0% was recorded in December 2017, and its highest, 22.0%, in April 2020.[[250]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-:9-258) In 2025, 99.3% of Hawaii's businesses were [small businesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_business "Small business"), employing 49.6% of the state's workforce.[[251]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-259)

In 2009, the United States military spent US$12.2 billion in Hawaii, accounting for 18% of spending in the state for that year. 75,000 United States Department of Defense personnel live in Hawaii.[[252]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-260) According to a 2013 study by Phoenix Marketing International, Hawaii at that time had the fourth-largest number of millionaires per capita in the United States, with a ratio of 7.2%.[[253]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-261)

### Taxation

Tax is collected by the Hawaii Department of Taxation.[[254]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-262) Most government revenue comes from [personal income taxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Income_tax "Income tax") and a [general excise tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_receipts_tax "Gross receipts tax") (GET) levied primarily on businesses; there is no statewide tax on sales,[[255]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-263) personal property, or stock transfers,[[256]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-264) while the effective property tax rate is among the lowest in the country.[[257]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-265) The high rate of tourism means that millions of visitors generate public revenue through GET and the hotel room tax.[[258]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-taxes-266) However, Hawaii residents generally pay among the most state taxes per person in the U.S.[[258]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-taxes-266)

The Tax Foundation of Hawaii considers the state's tax burden too high, claiming that it contributes to higher prices and the perception of an unfriendly business climate.[[258]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-taxes-266) The nonprofit Tax Foundation ranks Hawaii third in income tax burden and second in its overall tax burden, though notes that a significant portion of taxes are borne by tourists.[[259]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-267) Former [State Senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_Senate "Hawaii Senate")[Sam Slom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Slom "Sam Slom") attributed Hawaii's comparatively high tax rate to the fact that the state government is responsible for education, health care, and social services that are usually handled at a county or municipal level in most other states.[[258]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-taxes-266)

### Cost of living

The cost of living in Hawaii, specifically Honolulu, is high compared to that of most major U.S. cities, although it is 6.7% lower than in New York City and 3.6% lower than in San Francisco.[[260]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-268) These numbers may not take into account some costs, such as increased travel costs for flights, additional shipping fees, and the loss of promotional participation opportunities for customers outside the contiguous U.S. While some online stores offer free shipping on orders to Hawaii, many merchants exclude Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico and certain other U.S. territories.[[261]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-269)[[262]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-270)

[Hawaiian Electric Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_Electric_Industries "Hawaiian Electric Industries"), a privately owned company, provides 95% of the state's population with electricity, mostly from fossil-fuel power stations. Average electricity prices in October 2014 (36.41 cents per kilowatt-hour) were nearly three times the national average (12.58 cents per kilowatt-hour) and 80% higher than the second-highest state, Connecticut.[[263]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-271)

Median housing prices by State

The median home value in Hawaii in the 2000 U.S. Census was US$272,700, while the national median home value was US$119,600. Hawaii home values were the highest of all states, including California with a median home value of US$211,500.[[264]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-272) Research from the [National Association of Realtors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_of_Realtors "National Association of Realtors") places the 2010 median sale price of a single family home in Honolulu, Hawaii, at US$607,600 and the U.S. median sales price at US$173,200. The sale price of single family homes in Hawaii was the highest of any U.S. city in 2010, just above that of the Silicon Valley area of California (US$602,000).[[265]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-273)

Hawaii's very high [cost of living](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cost_of_living "Cost of living") is the result of several interwoven factors of the global economy in addition to domestic U.S. government trade policy. Like other regions with desirable weather year-round, such as California, [Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona "Arizona") and Florida, Hawaii's residents can be considered to be subject to a "[sunshine tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunshine_tax "Sunshine tax")". This situation is further exacerbated by the natural factors of geography and world distribution that lead to higher prices for goods due to increased shipping costs, a problem which many [island states and territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_country "Island country") suffer from as well.

The higher costs to ship goods across an ocean may be further increased by the requirements of the [Jones Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merchant_Marine_Act_of_1920 "Merchant Marine Act of 1920"), which generally requires that goods be transported between places within the U.S., including between the mainland U.S. west coast and Hawaii, using only U.S.-owned, built, and crewed ships. Jones Act-compliant vessels are often more expensive to build and operate than foreign equivalents, which can drive up shipping costs. While the Jones Act does not affect transportation of goods to Hawaii directly from Asia, this type of trade is nonetheless not common; this is a result of other primarily economic reasons including additional costs associated with stopping over in Hawaii (e.g. pilot and port fees), the market size of Hawaii, and the economics of using ever-larger ships that cannot be handled in Hawaii for transoceanic voyages. Therefore, Hawaii relies on receiving most inbound goods on Jones Act-qualified vessels originating from the U.S. west coast, which may contribute to the increased cost of some consumer goods and therefore the overall cost of living.[[266]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Keeping_up_with_the_Jones_Act-274)[[267]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-U.S._Law_Restricting_Foreign_Ships_Leads_to_Higher_Gas_Prices-275) Critics of the Jones Act contend that Hawaii consumers ultimately bear the expense of transporting goods imposed by the Jones Act.[[268]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Star-Bulletin_on_Jones_Act-276)

## Culture

The aboriginal culture of Hawaii is Polynesian. Hawaii represents the northernmost extension of the vast [Polynesian Triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_Triangle "Polynesian Triangle") of the south and central Pacific Ocean. While traditional Hawaiian culture remains as vestiges in modern Hawaiian society, there are re-enactments of the ceremonies and traditions throughout the islands. Some of these cultural influences, including the popularity (in greatly modified form) of _[lūʻau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luau "Luau")_ and _[hula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hula "Hula")_, and gestures such as the [Shaka sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaka_sign "Shaka sign"), are strong enough to affect the wider United States.

### Cuisine

[![Image 38: A painting of a man carrying taro by a yoke.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/71/Man_with_a_Yoke_Carrying_Taro_by_Joseph_Strong%2C_oil_on_canvas_board%2C_1880%2C_Honolulu_Museum_of_Art%2C_accession_12692.1.JPG/250px-Man_with_a_Yoke_Carrying_Taro_by_Joseph_Strong%2C_oil_on_canvas_board%2C_1880%2C_Honolulu_Museum_of_Art%2C_accession_12692.1.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Man_with_a_Yoke_Carrying_Taro_by_Joseph_Strong,_oil_on_canvas_board,_1880,_Honolulu_Museum_of_Art,_accession_12692.1.JPG)

[Taro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taro "Taro"), or in Hawaiian _kalo_, was one of the primary staples in Ancient Hawaii and remains a central ingredient in Hawaiian gastronomy today.

The [cuisine of Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuisine_of_Hawaii "Cuisine of Hawaii") is a fusion of many foods brought by immigrants to the Hawaiian Islands, including the earliest Polynesians and [Native Hawaiian cuisine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Hawaiian_cuisine "Native Hawaiian cuisine"), and [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuisine_of_the_United_States "Cuisine of the United States"), [Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_cuisine "Chinese cuisine"), [Filipino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_cuisine "Philippine cuisine"), [Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_cuisine "Japanese cuisine"), [Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_cuisine "Korean cuisine"), [Polynesian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_cuisine "Polynesian cuisine"), [Puerto Rican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rican_cuisine "Puerto Rican cuisine"), and [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_cuisine "Portuguese cuisine") origins. Plant and animal food sources are imported from around the world for agricultural use in Hawaii. _[Poi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poi\_(Hawaiian\_food) "Poi (Hawaiian food)")_, a starch made by pounding [taro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taro "Taro"), is one of the traditional foods of the islands. Many local restaurants serve the ubiquitous [plate lunch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_lunch "Plate lunch"), which features two scoops of rice, a simplified version of American [macaroni salad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macaroni_salad "Macaroni salad") and a variety of toppings including [hamburger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburger "Hamburger") patties, a fried egg, and [gravy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravy "Gravy") of a _[loco moco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loco\_moco "Loco moco")_, Japanese style _[tonkatsu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonkatsu "Tonkatsu")_ or the traditional lūʻau favorites, including _[kālua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalua "Kalua")_ pork and _[laulau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laulau "Laulau")_. _[Spam musubi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spam\_musubi "Spam musubi")_ is an example of the fusion of ethnic cuisine that developed on the islands among the mix of immigrant groups and military personnel. In the 1990s, a group of chefs developed [Hawaii regional cuisine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_regional_cuisine "Hawaii regional cuisine") as a contemporary fusion cuisine.

### Customs and etiquette

Some key customs and etiquette in Hawaii are as follows: when visiting a home, it is considered good manners to bring a small gift for one's host (for example, a dessert). Thus, parties are usually in the form of [potlucks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potluck "Potluck"). Most locals take their shoes off before entering a home. It is customary for Hawaiian families, regardless of ethnicity, to hold a luau[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] to celebrate a child's first birthday. It is also customary at Hawaiian weddings, especially at Filipino weddings, for the bride and groom to do a money dance (also called the [pandanggo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandanggo "Pandanggo")). Print media and local residents recommend that one refer to residents of Hawaii who are not ethnically Hawaiian as "locals of Hawaii" or "people of Hawaii".

### Hawaiian mythology

[![Image 39](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Ethnologisches_Museum_Dahlem_Berlin_Mai_2006_009.jpg/250px-Ethnologisches_Museum_Dahlem_Berlin_Mai_2006_009.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ethnologisches_Museum_Dahlem_Berlin_Mai_2006_009.jpg)

A stone carving of a Hawaiian deity, housed at a [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_Germany "Culture of Germany") museum

Hawaiian mythology includes the legends, historical tales, and sayings of the ancient Hawaiian people. It is considered a variant of a more general [Polynesian mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_mythology "Polynesian mythology") that developed a unique character for several centuries before c. 1800. It is associated with the [Hawaiian religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_religion "Hawaiian religion"), which was officially suppressed in the 19th century but was kept alive by some practitioners to the modern day.[[269]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-277) Prominent figures and terms include [Aumakua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aumakua "Aumakua"), the spirit of an ancestor or family god and [Kāne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C4%81ne "Kāne"), the highest of the four major Hawaiian deities.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Polynesian mythology

[![Image 40](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Tahiti-Oro.jpg/250px-Tahiti-Oro.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tahiti-Oro.jpg)

A sacred god figure wrapping for the war god ['Oro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%27Oro "'Oro"), made of woven dried coconut fibre ([sennit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sennit "Sennit")), made to protect a Polynesian god effigy (_to'o_), carved from wood

Polynesian mythology is the [oral traditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oral_tradition "Oral tradition") of the people of Polynesia, a grouping of Central and South Pacific Ocean island [archipelagos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archipelago "Archipelago") in the [Polynesian triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_triangle "Polynesian triangle") together with the scattered cultures known as the [Polynesian outliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_outliers "Polynesian outliers"). Polynesians speak languages that descend from a language reconstructed as [Proto-Polynesian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Polynesian_language "Proto-Polynesian language") that was probably spoken in the area around [Tonga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonga "Tonga") and [Samoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samoa "Samoa") in around 1000 BC.[[270]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-278)

Prior to the 15th century, [Polynesian people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_culture "Polynesian culture") migrated east to the [Cook Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook_Islands "Cook Islands"), and from there to other island groups such as Tahiti and the [Marquesas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marquesas "Marquesas"). Their descendants later discovered the islands [Tahiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tahiti "Tahiti"), [Rapa Nui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapa_Nui "Rapa Nui"), and later the Hawaiian Islands and [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand").[[271]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-279)

The Polynesian languages are part of the [Austronesian language family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austronesian_language_family "Austronesian language family"). Many are close enough in terms of vocabulary and grammar to be [mutually intelligible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutual_intelligibility "Mutual intelligibility"). There are also substantial cultural similarities between the various groups, especially in terms of social organization, childrearing, horticulture, building and textile technologies. Their mythologies in particular demonstrate local reworkings of commonly shared tales. The Polynesian cultures each have distinct but related oral traditions; legends or myths are traditionally considered to recount ancient history (the time of "pō") and the adventures of gods ("[atua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atua "Atua")") and deified ancestors.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

There are [many Hawaiian state parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Hawaiian_state_parks "List of Hawaiian state parks").

*   The [Island of Hawaiʻi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawai%CA%BBi_(island) "Hawaiʻi (island)") has state parks, recreation areas, and historical parks.
*   [Kauaʻi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaua%CA%BBi "Kauaʻi") has the Ahukini State Recreation Pier, six state parks, and the [Russian Fort Elizabeth State Historical Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Fort_Elizabeth_State_Historical_Park "Russian Fort Elizabeth State Historical Park").
*   [Maui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maui "Maui") has two state monuments, several state parks, and the [Polipoli Spring State Recreation Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polipoli_Spring_State_Recreation_Area "Polipoli Spring State Recreation Area"). [Moloka'i](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moloka%27i "Moloka'i") has the [Pala'au State Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pala%27au_State_Park "Pala'au State Park").
*   [Oʻahu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O%CA%BBahu "Oʻahu") has several state parks, a number of state recreation areas, and a number of monuments, including the [Ulu Pō Heiau State Monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulu_P%C5%8D_Heiau_State_Monument "Ulu Pō Heiau State Monument").

Different types of [ukuleles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukulele "Ukulele"), widely used in Hawaiian music

[![Image 42](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Bonnaroo08_jackjohnson2_lg.jpg/250px-Bonnaroo08_jackjohnson2_lg.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bonnaroo08_jackjohnson2_lg.jpg)

[Jack Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Johnson_(musician) "Jack Johnson (musician)"), a folk rock musician, was born and raised on [Oʻahu's North Shore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Shore_(O%CA%BBahu) "North Shore (Oʻahu)").

The music of Hawaii includes traditional and popular styles, ranging from native Hawaiian folk music to modern rock and [hip hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip_hop_music "Hip hop music").

Styles such as [slack-key guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slack-key_guitar "Slack-key guitar") are well known worldwide, while Hawaiian-tinged music is a frequent part of [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_the_United_States "Cinema of the United States") soundtracks. Hawaii also made a major contribution to [country music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") with the introduction of the [steel guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel_guitar "Steel guitar").[[272]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Unterberger-280)

Traditional Hawaiian folk music is a major part of the state's musical heritage. The Hawaiian people have inhabited the islands for centuries and have retained much of their traditional musical knowledge. Their music is largely religious in nature, and includes chanting and dance music.

Hawaiian music has had an enormous impact on the [music of other Polynesian islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesian_music "Polynesian music"); according to Peter Manuel, the influence of Hawaiian music is a "unifying factor in the development of modern Pacific musics".[[273]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Manuel-281) Native Hawaiian musician and Hawaiian sovereignty activist [Israel Kamakawiwoʻole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Kamakawiwo%CA%BBole "Israel Kamakawiwoʻole"), famous for his medley of "[Somewhere Over the Rainbow/What a Wonderful World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somewhere_Over_the_Rainbow/What_a_Wonderful_World "Somewhere Over the Rainbow/What a Wonderful World")", was named "The Voice of Hawaii" by [NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR") in 2010 in its 50 great voices series.[[274]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-282)

### Sports

Due to its distance from the continental United States, team sports in Hawaii are characterised by youth, collegial and amateur teams over professional teams, although some professional teams sports teams have at one time played in the state. Notable professional teams include [The Hawaiians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hawaiians_(WFL) "The Hawaiians (WFL)"), which played at the [World Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Football_League "World Football League") in 1974 and 1975; the [Hawaii Islanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_Islanders "Hawaii Islanders"), a Triple-A minor league baseball team that played at the [Pacific Coast League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Coast_League "Pacific Coast League") from 1961 to 1987; and [Team Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Team_Hawaii "Team Hawaii"), a [North American Soccer League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_Soccer_League_(1968%E2%80%9384) "North American Soccer League (1968–84)") team that played in 1977.

Notable college sports events in Hawaii include the [Maui Invitational Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maui_Invitational_Tournament "Maui Invitational Tournament"), [Diamond Head Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamond_Head_Classic "Diamond Head Classic") (basketball) and [Hawaii Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_Bowl "Hawaii Bowl") (football). The only [NCAA Division I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I "NCAA Division I") team in Hawaii is the [Hawaii Rainbow Warriors and Rainbow Wahine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_Rainbow_Warriors_and_Rainbow_Wahine "Hawaii Rainbow Warriors and Rainbow Wahine"), which competes at the [Big West Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_West_Conference "Big West Conference") (major sports), [Mountain West Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_West_Conference "Mountain West Conference") (football) and [Mountain Pacific Sports Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_Pacific_Sports_Federation "Mountain Pacific Sports Federation") (minor sports). There are three teams in NCAA Division II: [Chaminade Silverswords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaminade_Silverswords "Chaminade Silverswords"), [Hawaii Pacific Sharks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_Pacific_Sharks "Hawaii Pacific Sharks") and Hawaii-Hilo Vulcans, all of which compete at the [Pacific West Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_West_Conference "Pacific West Conference").

[Punaluʻu Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punalu%CA%BBu_Beach "Punaluʻu Beach"), on the Big Island features black volcanic sand.

Tourism is an important part of the Hawaiian economy as it represents a quarter of the economy. According to the Hawaii Tourism: 2019 Annual Visitor Research Report, a total of 10,386,673 visitors arrived in 2019 which increased 5% from the previous year, with expenditures of almost $18 billion.[[275]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-283) In 2019, tourism provided over 216,000 jobs statewide and contributed more than $2 billion in tax revenue.[[276]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-284) Due to mild year-round weather, tourist travel is popular throughout the year. Tourists across the globe visited Hawaii in 2019 with over 1 million tourists from the U.S. East, almost 2 million Japanese tourists, and almost 500,000 Canadian tourists.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

It was with statehood in 1959 that the Hawaii tourism industry began to grow.[[277]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-:6-285)

According to Hawaiian scholar [Haunani-Kay Trask](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haunani-Kay_Trask "Haunani-Kay Trask"), tourism in Hawaii has led to the commodification and exploitation of Hawaiian culture resulting in insidious forms of "cultural prostitution". Hawaii has been used to fuel ideas of escapism yet tourism in Hawaii ignores the harm Kanaka and locals experience.[[278]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-TraskBL-286) Cultural traditions such as the hula have been made "ornamental... a form of exotica" for tourists as a way for large corporations and land owners to gain profit over the exploitation of Hawaiian people and culture.[[278]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-TraskBL-286)

Tourism in Hawaii has been considered as an escape from reality resulting in the dismissal of violence faced by Native Hawaiians and locals living on the land. According to scholar [Winona LaDuke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winona_LaDuke "Winona LaDuke"), native Hawaiians have been forced to gather "shrimp and fish from ponds sitting on resort property".[[279]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-287) Tourism has also had damaging effects on the environment such as water shortages, overcrowding, sea level rising, elevated sea surface temperatures and micro plastics on beaches.[[280]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-288)[[281]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-289)[[282]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-290)

Due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), tourism in Hawaii came to a halt, which allowed the land, water, and animals to began to heal. Fish such as the baby akule and big ulua returned after years of not being around the bay. The coral reefs, fish, water growth, and [limu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limu_(algae) "Limu (algae)") (algae) growth was able to flourish without the impact of tourism.[[283]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-291)

There has been pushback against tourism by Native Hawaiians, urging people not to visit the islands. A survey by the Hawaii Tourism Authority indicated over two-thirds of Hawaiians did not want tourists to return to Hawaii. Tourism had "become extractive and hurtful, with tourists coming here and taking, taking, taking, taking, without any reciprocation with locals".[[284]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-292)

Hawaii hosts numerous cultural events. The annual [Merrie Monarch Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrie_Monarch_Festival "Merrie Monarch Festival") is an international Hula competition.[[285]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-293) The [Hawaii International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_International_Film_Festival "Hawaii International Film Festival") is the premier film festival for Pacific rim cinema.[[286]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Shane_Nelson-294) Honolulu hosts the state's long-running LGBT film festival, the [Honolulu Rainbow Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honolulu_Rainbow_Film_Festival "Honolulu Rainbow Film Festival").[[287]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-295)[[288]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-296)

## Health

As of 2009, Hawaii's health care system insures 92% of residents. Under the state's plan, businesses are required to provide insurance to employees who work more than twenty hours per week. Heavy regulation of insurance companies helps reduce the cost to employers. Due in part to heavy emphasis on preventive care, Hawaiians' total health care expenses measured as a percentage of state GDP are substantially lower.[[289]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-297) Proponents of [universal health care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_health_care "Universal health care") elsewhere in the U.S. sometimes use Hawaii as a model for proposed federal and state health care plans.[[290]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-298)

## Education

### Public schools

[![Image 46: Façade of a public high school.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/Waianae_High_School_%285888481033%29.jpg/250px-Waianae_High_School_%285888481033%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Waianae_High_School_(5888481033).jpg)

[Waianae High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waianae_High_School "Waianae High School"), located in [Waiʻanae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waianae,_Hawaii "Waianae, Hawaii"), houses an educational community media center

Hawaii has the only school system within the U.S. that is unified statewide. Policy decisions are made by the fourteen-member state [Board of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_Board_of_Education "Hawaii Board of Education"), which sets policy and hires the superintendent of schools, who oversees the [Hawaii Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_Department_of_Education "Hawaii Department of Education"). The Department of Education is divided into seven districts; four on Oʻahu and one for each of the other three counties.

Public elementary, middle and high school test scores in Hawaii are below national averages on tests mandated under the [No Child Left Behind Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Child_Left_Behind_Act "No Child Left Behind Act"). The Hawaii Board of Education requires all eligible students to take these tests and report all student test scores. This may have unbalanced the results that reported in August 2005 that of 282 schools across the state, 185 failed to reach federal minimum performance standards in mathematics and reading.[[291]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-299) The [ACT college placement tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACT_(examination) "ACT (examination)") show that in 2005, seniors scored slightly above the national average (21.9 compared with 20.9),[[292]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-300) but in the widely accepted [SAT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAT "SAT") examinations, Hawaii's college-bound seniors tend to score below the national average in all categories except mathematics.

The first native controlled public charter school was the [Kanu O Ka Aina New Century Charter School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanu_O_Ka_Aina_New_Century_Charter_School "Kanu O Ka Aina New Century Charter School").[[293]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-301)

### Private schools

Hawaii has the highest rates of private school attendance in the nation. During the 2011–2012 school year, Hawaii public and charter schools had an enrollment of 181,213,[[294]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-DOE-302) while private schools had 37,695.[[295]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-HAIS-303) Private schools educated over 17% of students in Hawaii that school year, nearly three times the approximate national average of 6%.[[296]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-NCES-304) According to Alia Wong of _[Honolulu Civil Beat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honolulu\_Civil\_Beat "Honolulu Civil Beat")_, this is due to private schools being relatively inexpensive compared to ones on the mainland as well as the overall reputations of private schools.[[297]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-305)

It has four of the largest independent schools; [ʻIolani School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iolani_School "Iolani School"), [Kamehameha Schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamehameha_Schools "Kamehameha Schools"), [Mid-Pacific Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-Pacific_Institute "Mid-Pacific Institute") and [Punahou School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punahou_School "Punahou School"). [Pacific Buddhist Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Buddhist_Academy "Pacific Buddhist Academy"), the second Buddhist high school in the U.S. and first such school in Hawaii, was founded in 2003.

Independent schools can select their students, while most public schools of HIDOE are open to all students in their attendance zones. The Kamehameha Schools are the only schools in the U.S. that openly grant admission to students based on ancestry; collectively, they are one of the wealthiest schools in the United States, if not the world, having over eleven billion US dollars in estate assets.[[298]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-306) In 2005, Kamehameha enrolled 5,398 students, 8.4% of the Native Hawaiian children in the state.[[299]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-307)

Main entrance of the [University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Hawai%CA%BBi_at_M%C4%81noa "University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa")

The largest institution of higher learning in Hawaii is the [University of Hawaiʻi System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Hawai%CA%BBi_System "University of Hawaiʻi System"), which consists of the research university at [Mānoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Hawai%CA%BBi_at_M%C4%81noa "University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa"), two comprehensive campuses at [Hilo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Hawai%CA%BBi_at_Hilo "University of Hawaiʻi at Hilo") and [West Oʻahu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Hawai%CA%BBi_at_West_O%CA%BBahu "University of Hawaiʻi at West Oʻahu"), and seven community colleges. Private universities include [Brigham Young University–Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University%E2%80%93Hawaii "Brigham Young University–Hawaii"), [Chaminade University of Honolulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaminade_University_of_Honolulu "Chaminade University of Honolulu"), [Hawaii Pacific University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_Pacific_University "Hawaii Pacific University"), and [Wayland Baptist University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayland_Baptist_University "Wayland Baptist University"). [Saint Stephen Diocesan Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Stephen_Diocesan_Seminary,_Honolulu "Saint Stephen Diocesan Seminary, Honolulu") is a [seminary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seminary "Seminary") of the [Roman Catholic Diocese of Honolulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Diocese_of_Honolulu "Roman Catholic Diocese of Honolulu"). Kona hosts the [University of the Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Nations "University of the Nations"), which is not an [accredited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Educational_accreditation "Educational accreditation") university.

## Transportation

[![Image 48](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Daniel_K._Inouye_International_Airport_Air_Traffic_Control_Tower_2025.jpg/250px-Daniel_K._Inouye_International_Airport_Air_Traffic_Control_Tower_2025.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Daniel_K._Inouye_International_Airport_Air_Traffic_Control_Tower_2025.jpg)

Daniel K. Inouye International Airport

A [system of state highways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Hawaii_state_highways "List of Hawaii state highways") encircles each main island. Only Oʻahu has federal highways, and is the only area outside the contiguous 48 states to have signed [Interstate highways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_Highway_System "Interstate Highway System"). Narrow, winding roads and congestion in populated places can slow traffic. Each major island has a public bus system.

[Daniel K. Inouye International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_K._Inouye_International_Airport "Daniel K. Inouye International Airport") ([IATA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Air_Transport_Association_airport_code "International Air Transport Association airport code"):HNL), which shares runways with the adjacent [Hickam Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hickam_Field "Hickam Field") (IATA:HIK), is the major commercial aviation hub of Hawaii. The airport was previously known as Honolulu International Airport, before its official renaming on May 30, 2017, after the late U.S. Senator [Daniel K. Inouye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Inouye "Daniel Inouye").[[300]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-308) The commercial aviation airport offers intercontinental service to North America, Asia, Australia and Oceania. [Hawaiian Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_Airlines "Hawaiian Airlines") and [Mokulele Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mokulele_Airlines "Mokulele Airlines") use jets to provide services between the large airports in Honolulu, Līhuʻe, Kahului, Kona and Hilo. These airlines also provide air freight services between the islands.

Until air passenger services began in the 1920s,[[301]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Hawaii_Aviation-309) private boats were the sole means of traveling between the islands. Seaflite operated [hydrofoils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrofoils "Hydrofoils") between the major islands in the mid-1970s.[[302]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-310)

The [Hawaii Superferry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_Superferry "Hawaii Superferry") operated between Oʻahu and Maui between December 2007 and March 2009, with additional routes planned for other islands. Protests and legal problems over environmental impact statements ended the service, though the company operating Superferry has expressed a wish to recommence ferry services in the future.[[303]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Alakai-311) Currently there is a passenger ferry service in [Maui County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maui_County "Maui County") between Lanaʻi and Maui,[[304]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Lana'i_Ferry-312) which does not take vehicles; a passenger ferry to Molokaʻi ended in 2016.[[305]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-313) Currently [Norwegian Cruise Lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Cruise_Lines "Norwegian Cruise Lines") and [Princess Cruises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Cruises "Princess Cruises") provide passenger cruise ship services between the larger islands.[[306]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-NCL-314)[[307]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-Princess_Cruises-315)

### Rail

At one time Hawaii had a network of railroads on each of the larger islands that transported farm commodities and passengers. Most were 3 ft (914 mm) [narrow gauge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narrow_gauge "Narrow gauge") systems but there were some 2 ft 6 in (762 mm) gauge on some of the smaller islands. The standard gauge in the U.S. is 4 ft 8+1⁄2 in (1,435 mm). By far the largest railroad was the [Oahu Railway and Land Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oahu_Railway_and_Land_Company "Oahu Railway and Land Company") (OR&L) that ran lines from Honolulu across the western and northern part of Oʻahu.[[308]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-ReferenceA-316)

The OR&L was important for moving troops and goods during World War II. Traffic on this line was busy enough for signals to be used to facilitate movement of trains and to require [wigwag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wigwag_(railroad) "Wigwag (railroad)") signals at some railroad crossings for the protection of motorists. The main line was officially abandoned in 1947, although part of it was bought by the U.S. Navy and operated until 1970. Thirteen miles (21 km) of track remain; preservationists occasionally run trains over a portion of this line.[[308]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-ReferenceA-316)

[Skyline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skyline_(Honolulu) "Skyline (Honolulu)") is an elevated passenger rail line operated by [HART](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honolulu_Authority_for_Rapid_Transportation "Honolulu Authority for Rapid Transportation"), a semi-autonomous agency of the [City and County of Honolulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honolulu_County,_Hawaii "Honolulu County, Hawaii"). It was built with the intention to relieve highway congestion.[[309]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-317) A portion of Skyline opened for service in 2023, with the next phase expected to open in October 2025, and the final phase in 2031.[[310]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-318)

## Governance

### Political subdivisions and local government

[![Image 49](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/Washington_Place_Honolulu_HI.jpg/250px-Washington_Place_Honolulu_HI.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Washington_Place_Honolulu_HI.jpg)

The [Governor of Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Hawaii "Governor of Hawaii") officially resides at [Washington Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Place "Washington Place"), an old American-built residence

The movement of the Hawaiian royal family from Hawaiʻi Island to Maui, and subsequently to Oʻahu, explains the modern-day distribution of population centers. [Kamehameha III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamehameha_III "Kamehameha III") chose the largest city, Honolulu, as his capital because of its natural harbor—the present-day [Honolulu Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honolulu_Harbor "Honolulu Harbor"). Now the state capital, Honolulu is located along the southeast coast of Oʻahu. The previous capital was [Lahaina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahaina,_Hawaii "Lahaina, Hawaii"), Maui, and before that [Kailua-Kona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kailua-Kona "Kailua-Kona"), Hawaiʻi. Some major towns are [Hilo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilo,_Hawaii "Hilo, Hawaii"); [Kaneohe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaneohe,_Hawaii "Kaneohe, Hawaii"); [Kailua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kailua,_Honolulu_County,_Hawaii "Kailua, Honolulu County, Hawaii"); [Pearl City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_City,_Hawaii "Pearl City, Hawaii"); [Waipahu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waipahu,_Hawaii "Waipahu, Hawaii"); [Kahului](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kahului,_Hawaii "Kahului, Hawaii"); [Kailua-Kona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kailua,_Hawaii_County,_Hawaii "Kailua, Hawaii County, Hawaii"). [Kīhei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kihei,_Hawaii "Kihei, Hawaii"); and [Līhuʻe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lihue,_Hawaii "Lihue, Hawaii").

Hawaii has five counties: the [City and County of Honolulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honolulu_County,_Hawaii "Honolulu County, Hawaii"), [Hawaiʻi County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawai%CA%BBi_County,_Hawaii "Hawaiʻi County, Hawaii"), [Maui County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maui_County,_Hawaii "Maui County, Hawaii"), [Kauaʻi County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaua%CA%BBi_County,_Hawaii "Kauaʻi County, Hawaii"), and [Kalawao County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalawao_County,_Hawaii "Kalawao County, Hawaii").

Hawaii has the fewest local governments among U.S. states.[[311]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-USCensus2010-319)[[312]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-USCensus2007-320) Unique to this state is the lack of [municipal governments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipal_corporation "Municipal corporation"). All local governments are generally administered at the [county](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_(United_States) "County (United States)") level. The only incorporated area in the state is [Honolulu County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honolulu_County,_Hawaii "Honolulu County, Hawaii"), a [consolidated city–county](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consolidated_city%E2%80%93county "Consolidated city–county") that governs the entire island of Oʻahu. County executives are referred to as mayors; these are the [Mayor of Hawaiʻi County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Hawai%CA%BBi_County "Mayor of Hawaiʻi County"), [Mayor of Honolulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Honolulu "Mayor of Honolulu"), [Mayor of Kauaʻi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Kaua%CA%BBi "Mayor of Kauaʻi"), and the [Mayor of Maui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Maui "Mayor of Maui"). The mayors are all elected in [nonpartisan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-partisan_democracy "Non-partisan democracy") elections. Kalawao County has no elected government,[[313]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-321) and as [mentioned above](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#Education) there are no local [school districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_district "School district"); instead, all local public education is administered at the state level by the [Hawaii Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_Department_of_Education "Hawaii Department of Education"). The remaining local governments are [special districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special-purpose_district "Special-purpose district").[[311]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-USCensus2010-319)[[312]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii#cite_note-USCensus2007-320)

### State government

[![Image 50](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/Hawaii_State_Capitol%2C_Honolulu.jpg/250px-Hawaii_State_Capitol%2C_Honolulu.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hawaii_State_Capitol,_Honolulu.jpg)

[Hawaii State Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_State_Capitol "Hawaii State Capitol") building

The state government of Hawaii is modeled after the federal government with adaptations originating from the kingdom era of Hawaiian history. As codified in the [Constitution of Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Hawaii "Constitution of Hawaii"), there are three [branches of government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Branches_of_government "Branches of government"): executive, legislative, and judicial, although the [Office of Hawaiian Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_Hawaiian_Affairs "Office of Hawaiian Affairs") is often referred to as the fourth branch of government as it does not fall under the other three branches. The executive branch is led by the [Governor of Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Hawaii "Governor of Hawaii"), who is assisted by the [Lieutenant Governor of Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_Governor_of_Hawaii "Lieutenant Governor of Hawaii"), both of whom are elected on the same ticket. The governor is the only state public official elected statewide; all others are appointed by the governor. The lieutenant governor acts as the [Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_of_Hawaii "Secretary of State of Hawaii"). The governor and lieutenant governor oversee twenty agencies and departments from offices in the [State Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_State_Capitol "Hawaii State Capitol"). The official residence of the governor is [Washington Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Place "Washington Place").

The legislative branch consists of the [bicameral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicameralism "Bicameralism")[Hawaii State Legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_State_Legislature "Hawaii State Legislature"), which is composed of the 51-member [Hawaii House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_House_of_Representatives "Hawaii House of Representatives") led by the [Speaker of the House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_(politics) "Speaker (politics)"), and the 25-member [Hawaii Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_Senate "Hawaii Senate") led by the [President of the Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Senate "President of the Senate"). The Legislature meets at the [State Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_State_Capitol "Hawaii State Capitol"). The unified judicial branch of Hawaii is the [Hawaii State Judiciary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_State_Judiciary "Hawaii State Judiciary"). The [state's highest court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_supreme_court "State supreme court") is the [Supreme Court of Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Hawaii "Supreme Court of Hawaii"), which uses [Aliʻiōlani Hale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aliiolani_Hale "Aliiolani Hale") as its chambers.

Hawaii is represented in the [United States Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") by two senators and two [representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives"). Former representative [Ed Case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Case "Ed Case") was elected in 2018 to the [1st congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii%27s_1st_congressional_district "Hawaii's 1st congressional district").
